paras: The Ashland mob attack on the Granite State took place on November 1, 1882, when a mob at Ashland, Kentucky, tried to seize William Neal and Ellis Craft, prisoners accused of murder, from State Guard troops carrying them down the Ohio River. The troops fired on the mob's ferryboat and on the crowd watching from the bank, killing five or six townspeople, while the prisoners reached jail unharmed. A coroner's jury held the troops' commander culpable for the killings.

Neal and Craft had been convicted at Catlettsburg of murdering Robert and Fannie Gibbons and Emma Carrier at Ashland in December 1881, but were granted a new trial; an alleged accomplice, George Ellis, had been hanged by a mob at Ashland that summer. About 220 State Guards under Major John R. Allen brought the prisoners to Catlettsburg on October 30, and the next day Judge George N. Brown moved the trial to Carter County. That night a mob at Ashland searched trains and tore up railroad track.

Around noon on November 1 a trainload of men from Ashland reached Catlettsburg, and a committee demanded the prisoners from Allen, who refused. According to the Maysville Evening Bulletin, the leader said the mob meant to hang them and warned that Allen "would catch hell at Ashland." The troops boarded the steamer Granite State with the prisoners, and the mob raced back by train, firing at the boat along the way.

At Ashland a party of men and boys seized the ferryboat, by one account with a pistol at the captain's head, and steamed out to intercept the steamer. When the Granite State passed, shots came from the ferryboat and the soldiers answered with volley after volley, disabling its boiler and striking the crowd of men, women and children on the bank and in nearby buildings. The steamer landed the prisoners at Maysville early on November 2, and they were taken on to the Lexington jail.

The dead included Colonel Lewis Reppard, about seventy, shot on the bank; George Keener; an infant in its mother's arms; James McDonald, shot on the ferryboat; and Alex. Harris, who died November 3. Among the wounded was Martin Green, the only person the lists identify by race, as "colored."

At the coroner's inquest the Granite State's captain and express messenger testified that the ferryboat party numbered twenty or twenty-five and that the firing after the first volley was needless. The jury found that the militia's firing was not in the line of duty and held Allen culpable. Governor Luke P. Blackburn approved the troops' conduct and thanked them in special orders, while Judge Brown left home for Frankfort for fear of the mob.

A detective named two men who had demanded the prisoners, but no report of an arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage. Through December papers reported fears of bloodshed at the February trial in Grayson, while Carter County citizens promised a fair trial without troops.

White papers from Kentucky to Maine and the Indian Territory carried the story, mostly through Cincinnati, Ironton and Ashland dispatches that printed both the troops' and the townspeople's versions. Headlines called the mob "Western Lynchers Fighting For Their Prey" and "Would-be Lynchers" and treated the "Ashland murderers" as guilty.

The Maysville Evening Bulletin, whose home company served in the battalion, printed a poem beginning "All honor to the soldiery," and the South Kentuckian held that the soldiers had acted on the defensive. Ashland correspondents instead called the firing on spectators "most wanton and unprovoked," and the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic headlined "Massacred by Soldiers!" and mocked Allen's report. No paper in the coverage gave the race of the prisoners or of the dead.

Allen reported that the ferryboat party fired two or three volleys and wounded two soldiers before he ordered fire, and the steamer's pilot said shots also came from the bank. Ashland accounts and sworn inquest testimony described one or two shots, none from shore, and only a grazed soldier and a scratched drummer. Death counts ranged from two men and a child in the first Ashland report to eight or ten in early wire stories.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: An armed mob demanded William Neal and Ellis Craft from the State Guard, avowed it would hang them, and attacked the steamer carrying them; the prisoners were not taken and the dead were townspeople shot by the troops (A7, A8, A12, A24).

The mob, acting without authority and on the accusation of murder, tried to seize Neal and Craft to hang them, but the troops kept custody and landed them safely at Maysville (A8, A9, A13). Those killed were mob members and spectators shot by the State militia, which is an attempted lynching and a militia shooting, not a completed lynching (A12, A27).

The mob's demand, the ferryboat attack and the troops' deadly fire are reported independently by Ashland correspondents, the boat's officers, Maj. Allen and the coroner's jury, though they disagree on who fired first and how much (A12, A13, A16, A18, A27).

accounts.label: Maj. Allen's official report
accounts.gist: A mob claiming 2,000 men threatened to attack at Ashland, fired from the train, and fired two or three volleys from the ferryboat, wounding two soldiers, before he ordered the troops to fire.

accounts.label: Granite State officers (pilot and clerk)
accounts.gist: Shots came from the ferryboat, the wharf boat and the bank; six balls struck the pilot house, and the troops acted promptly and without malice.

accounts.label: Ashland correspondents
accounts.gist: A handful of boys and men on the ferryboat, one firing a small revolver, drew volley after volley, and the soldiers then turned their fire on spectators on the bank and in buildings.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury witnesses
accounts.gist: The boat's captain and express messenger testified under oath that the ferryboat party numbered 20-25, no shots came from shore, and firing after the first volley was uncalled for.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury verdict
accounts.gist: The dead were killed by the militia's bullets, the firing was not in the line of duty, and Maj. Allen was culpable.

framing.detail: The Maysville Evening Bulletin ran a poem 'All honor to the soldiery' and headlines on the 'Splendid Conduct of the Soldiery' against an 'Armed Mob'.
Ashland's citizen correspondent called the firing among the citizens 'most wanton and unprovoked'; the Highland Weekly News headed it 'Lynch Law' with troops firing on 'Innocent Spectators'.
The Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic headlined 'Massacred by Soldiers!', sided with the mob's aim of punishing the accused, and mocked Maj. Allen.
The South Kentuckian called the affair lamentable but held that the soldiers acted on the defensive; the Clarksville Chronicle said the popular verdict exonerated Allen.
National wire copy framed the mob as 'Would-be Lynchers' or 'Western Lynchers Fighting For Their Prey' and printed both sides.

Neal and Craft were accused of the December 1881 murder of Robert and Fannie Gibbons and Emma Carrier at Ashland; a first conviction was set aside and a new trial granted
